questions.stem: What is air?
options: A mixture of different gases
Only one gas, oxygen
Empty space with nothing in it
Only one gas, nitrogen

explain.why: Air has oxygen but also nitrogen and other gases.
Air is made of gases, which are matter.
Nitrogen is the most plentiful gas, but it is not the only one.

solution: Air is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.stem: Which gas makes up the largest part of air?
options: Water vapour
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide

explain.why: Water vapour is a small part of air and its amount changes.
Oxygen is about one fifth of air, so it is second.
Carbon dioxide is only a tiny part of air.

solution: About 78% of air is nitrogen.

questions.stem: A candle burns in a room. Which gas in the air does the flame use?
options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Water vapour

explain.why: Nitrogen does not help things burn.
Carbon dioxide does not support burning.
Water vapour does not help things burn.

solution: Burning needs oxygen.

questions.stem: Which gas in air do we need to stay alive?
options: Nitrogen
Water vapour
Carbon dioxide
Oxygen

explain.why: We breathe nitrogen in and out, but our bodies do not use it.
Our bodies do not need water vapour from air for respiration.
We give this out when we breathe out.

solution: Living things use oxygen for respiration.

questions.stem: Which gas turns limewater milky?
options: Oxygen in the air
Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Water vapour

explain.why: Oxygen does not change limewater.
Nitrogen does not change limewater.
Water vapour does not turn limewater milky.

solution: Carbon dioxide is the gas that makes limewater turn milky.

questions.stem: A green plant is placed in bright light. Which gas does it add to the air?
options: Smoke
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide

explain.why: Plants do not make smoke.
Plants do not make nitrogen.
In light, plants take in carbon dioxide to make food.

solution: Plants give out oxygen when they make food in light.

questions.stem: Water drops form on the outside of a cold glass of ice water. Which gas in the air formed these drops?
options: Nitrogen
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Water vapour

explain.why: Nitrogen stays as a gas on the cold glass.
Oxygen stays as a gas on the cold glass.
Carbon dioxide does not turn into water.

solution: Water vapour in the air cools and turns into drops of water on the cold glass.

questions.stem: Mira blows up a balloon. What does this show about air?
options: Air is always cold
Air takes up space
Air is a liquid
Air has no mass

explain.why: The balloon says nothing about temperature.
Air is a mixture of gases.
Air has mass, but a balloon does not show that.

solution: The balloon gets bigger as air fills it, so air takes up space.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists gases that are all found in air?
options: Oxygen, iron and nitrogen
Water vapour, salt and oxygen
Carbon dioxide, sand and nitrogen
Nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide

explain.why: Iron is a solid metal.
Salt is a solid.
Sand is a solid.

solution: Nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide are all gases in air.

questions.stem: About how much of air is oxygen?
options: About one fifth
About one half
A tiny amount, less than one hundredth
About four fifths

explain.why: Half is far too much. Nitrogen is the biggest part.
That is about the carbon dioxide.
Four fifths is about the amount of nitrogen.

solution: Oxygen is about 21%, which is about one fifth.

questions.stem: The pie chart shows the gases in air. Which slice stands for nitrogen?
options: None of the slices
R
P
Q

explain.why: Nitrogen is the largest part of air.
R is the smallest part.
Q is the second biggest part, which is oxygen.

solution: Nitrogen is about 78%, the biggest slice.

options: Q
R
P
P and R together

explain.why: R is far smaller than the amount of oxygen.
P is the biggest slice. Oxygen is not the most plentiful gas.
Oxygen is one gas and has one slice.

solution: Oxygen is about 21%, the second biggest slice.

options: Carbon dioxide and the other gases
Only nitrogen
Nitrogen and oxygen together
Only oxygen

explain.why: Nitrogen is the biggest part of air.
Those two make up almost all of air.
Oxygen is the second biggest part.

solution: Carbon dioxide and the remaining gases make up only a tiny part of air.

options: P and Q together
P
R
Q

explain.why: Only oxygen is needed for burning.
P is nitrogen, which does not support burning.
R is the small amount of other gases.

solution: Oxygen supports burning and is about 21% of air, the Q bar.

questions.stem: Which of these gases is found in the smallest amount in air?
options: Nitrogen
They are all the same amount
Carbon dioxide
Oxygen

explain.why: Nitrogen is the largest part.
The gases are in very different amounts.
Oxygen is about one fifth of air.

solution: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of air.

questions.stem: Why do we need to breathe in air?
options: To get water vapour so that we do not need to drink
To get carbon dioxide for our bodies to use
To fill our lungs so that they stay big
To get oxygen for our bodies to use

explain.why: We still need to drink water.
We give carbon dioxide out.
We breathe to take in oxygen, not just to fill space.

solution: The body uses oxygen from the air for respiration.

questions.stem: A cold can of drink is left on a table. Drops of water appear on its outside. Where did the water come from?
options: Water that the can made from the cold
Oxygen in the air that turned into water
Water that leaked through tiny holes in the can
Water vapour in the air

explain.why: Cold does not make water. Water vapour cools and forms drops.
Oxygen does not turn into water.
The can is sealed. The drops come from outside.

solution: Water vapour in the air touches the cold can and turns back into water.

questions.stem: Two identical candles are lit and covered by jars P and Q. Which candle goes out first?
options: The one under jar Q, because it has more oxygen
Both go out at the same time because the flames are the same
Neither, because a candle can burn with no air
The one under jar P, because there is less oxygen in it

explain.why: More oxygen lets a candle burn longer.
The amount of oxygen differs.
A flame needs oxygen.

solution: The small jar has less air and so less oxygen. The flame goes out sooner, when too little oxygen is left in the small jar.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about air is true?
options: Air has mass and takes up space
Air has no mass because we cannot see it
Air is made up of only oxygen
Air does not take up space

explain.why: We cannot see air, but it has mass.
Air is a mixture of gases.
A balloon filled with air shows that air takes up space.

solution: Air is a mixture of gases, so it is matter with mass that takes up space.

questions.stem: The table shows three gases in air. Which gas is oxygen?
options: Z
X and Y
Y
X

explain.why: Z is a tiny part and does not keep a candle burning, so it is carbon dioxide.
Only one gas keeps the candle burning.
X is the biggest part and does not keep a candle burning, so it is nitrogen.

solution: Only oxygen keeps a candle burning and it is about 21% of air.

questions.stem: Which of the following shows that air contains water vapour?
options: Water drops form on the outside of a cold glass
A candle goes out in a closed jar
A balloon gets bigger when we blow into it
Limewater turns milky when we breathe into it

explain.why: This shows that burning uses oxygen.
This shows that air takes up space.
This shows carbon dioxide.

solution: Water vapour cools and turns back into drops on a cold surface.

questions.stem: A mouse is sealed in a jar of air for a long time. Which gas in the jar goes down?
options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
All the gases go down equally
Carbon dioxide

explain.why: The mouse does not use nitrogen.
Only oxygen is used by the mouse.
The mouse gives out carbon dioxide, so it goes up.

solution: The mouse uses up oxygen in respiration.

questions.stem: Which gas does not support burning?
options: Oxygen from the air
Pure oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Air

explain.why: Oxygen is the gas that supports burning.
More oxygen makes a flame burn brighter.
Air contains oxygen, so a flame can burn in it.

solution: Carbon dioxide does not support burning.

questions.stem: A student breathes out through a straw into limewater. The limewater turns milky. Which gas is in the air we breathe out?
options: Nitrogen
Oxygen, which turns limewater milky
Water vapour
Carbon dioxide

explain.why: Nitrogen does not change limewater.
Exhaled air still has oxygen, but oxygen does not change limewater.
Water vapour does not turn limewater milky.

solution: Limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Tube X has fresh air pumped into limewater. Tube Y has air from the lungs blown into limewater. Y turns milky faster. What does this show?
options: Limewater reacts with oxygen in the air from the lungs
Air from the lungs has more carbon dioxide
Fresh air has no carbon dioxide at all but air from the lungs has some
Air from the lungs has no oxygen left in it, unlike fresh air

explain.why: Limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide.
Fresh air has a very small amount.
It has less oxygen, not none.

solution: More carbon dioxide turns limewater milky faster.

options: Air we breathe out has more oxygen than air we breathe in
Exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air
Air we breathe in has more carbon dioxide than air we breathe out
Air we breathe out has no carbon dioxide

explain.why: The table shows 16% against 21%.
The table shows 0.04% against 4%.
The table shows 4%.

solution: In the dark the plant uses oxygen in respiration and adds none.

Carbon dioxide takes the oxygen out of the candle wax

questions.stem: Animals and fires use up oxygen all the time, yet the amount of oxygen in air stays about the same. Which reason helps to explain this?
options: Nitrogen slowly changes into oxygen in the air
Green plants give out oxygen in light
Water vapour breaks down into oxygen in the air
Carbon dioxide changes into oxygen in the air

explain.why: Nitrogen does not change into oxygen.
This does not happen in air.
Plants use carbon dioxide, but air does not change it by itself.

solution: Plants return oxygen to the air.

questions.stem: Which statement about air is correct?
options: Air is a mixture of gases and its water vapour amount can change
Oxygen makes up about half of the air
Carbon dioxide is the second most plentiful gas in air
Nitrogen is needed for burning, so it is used up by a flame

explain.why: It is about one fifth.
Oxygen is second. Carbon dioxide is tiny.
Oxygen is the gas needed for burning.

solution: Air has fixed large parts but variable water vapour.

questions.stem: A student breathes in and out of a closed plastic bag for two minutes. What happens to the gases in the bag?
options: Both oxygen and carbon dioxide go down
Nitrogen goes down and oxygen goes up
Oxygen goes down and carbon dioxide goes up
Oxygen goes up and carbon dioxide goes down

explain.why: The student gives carbon dioxide to the bag.
Nitrogen stays about the same.
The student uses oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide.

solution: Respiration uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Gas in a jar was tested before and after a candle burned in it. How does the gas after burning compare with the gas before?
options: It has less nitrogen and more oxygen
It has the same amount of every gas
It has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
It has more oxygen and less carbon dioxide

explain.why: Nitrogen stays about the same.
Burning changes the gases.
Burning uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide.

solution: The candle used oxygen and gave out carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Limewater is used in the trough instead of water. After the candle goes out, the limewater inside the jar turns milky. What does this show?
options: Carbon dioxide was made by the candle
The limewater has reacted with the glass of the jar
The jar now contains more oxygen than it did before
The candle made nitrogen

explain.why: The change is due to carbon dioxide.
Burning uses oxygen.
Limewater does not test for nitrogen.

solution: Milky limewater means carbon dioxide.

The plant had no effect on oxygen
The plant added oxygen both in light and in the dark

In the dark the oxygen went down.

solution: Light gives a rise and dark gives a fall.

options: No, it also has nitrogen and some oxygen
Yes, because the splint goes out
Yes, because it turns limewater milky and puts the splint out
No, it is only nitrogen

explain.why: A flame can also go out with low oxygen.
Other gases in a mixture do not affect that test.
Nitrogen does not turn limewater milky.

solution: The jar still holds the nitrogen of the original air.

questions.stem: Which method shows that air we breathe out has water vapour?
options: Breathe onto a burning candle
Breathe into a balloon and measure its size after
Breathe onto a cold mirror and look for drops
Breathe into limewater and look for a milky colour

explain.why: This does not test for water vapour.
This shows that air takes up space.
This tests for carbon dioxide.

solution: Water vapour condenses on a cold mirror.

questions.stem: A candle burns under a jar standing on a table. After a while the flame goes out. Why?
options: The jar has too much oxygen
There was too little oxygen left in the jar to keep it burning
All the air in the jar has been used up
The nitrogen in the jar has been used up

explain.why: Extra oxygen makes the flame brighter.
Only some of the oxygen is used. The other gases stay in the jar.
Nitrogen is not used by a burning candle.

solution: A burning candle uses oxygen. When the oxygen left is too little, the flame goes out.

The candle wax turns into water that fills the jar from below
The burning candle used some of the oxygen, so there is less gas in the jar
The nitrogen in the jar is used up by the candle

explain.why: A flame does not push the water.
Candle wax does not turn into the water in the trough.
A candle does not use nitrogen.

It is all carbon dioxide, made by the burning candle
It is all nitrogen, as nothing else can stay in the jar
It still has some oxygen, but too little to keep the flame going

explain.why: A flame goes out while some oxygen is still left.
Most of the gas left is nitrogen.
Some oxygen and a little carbon dioxide are still there.

solution: The flame goes out when the oxygen is too low. Some oxygen is still left.

options: Carbon dioxide

Oxygen

solution: Burning uses oxygen from the air in the jar.

options: Jar A, because the plant takes in the oxygen
Both the same, because the plant takes no part
Jar B, because the plant adds carbon dioxide in light
Jar B, because the plant adds oxygen in light

explain.why: In bright light the plant gives out oxygen.
The plant changes the gases in the jar.
In light the plant takes in carbon dioxide.

solution: More oxygen lets the candle burn longer.

options: The candle used only some of the oxygen, and the other gases stayed in the jar
The water is too heavy for the air outside to push it any higher
The candle used up all the gases in the jar before it went out
The candle made new oxygen as it burned, which filled the space

explain.why: The amount of gas lost sets the rise.
Most of the gas in the jar remained.
A burning candle uses oxygen. It does not make it.

solution: Only some of the oxygen is used, and the rest of the gas stays in the jar.

options: The heart
The windpipe
The nose
The lungs

explain.why: The windpipe carries air to the lungs.
Air enters the body through the nose.
The lungs take oxygen from the air into the blood.

solution: The heart pumps blood to all parts of the body.

questions.stem: Which part of the respiratory system carries air from the nose to the lungs?
options: A blood vessel
The windpipe
The food pipe
The heart

explain.why: Blood vessels carry blood, not air.
The food pipe belongs to the digestive system.
The heart is part of the circulatory system and pumps blood.

solution: Air passes along the windpipe on its way to the lungs.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the lungs?
options: To take oxygen from the air into the blood
To carry digested food to the cells
To break food down into tiny pieces for the body
To pump blood to the whole body

explain.why: Blood carries digested food to the cells.
Breaking down food is done by the digestive system.
Pumping blood is the job of the heart.

solution: Oxygen from the air passes into the blood in the lungs.

questions.stem: Which part of the body carries blood to all other parts of the body?
options: Blood vessels
The windpipe
The nose
The stomach and gut

explain.why: The windpipe carries air, not blood.
The nose lets air into the body.
The stomach is part of the digestive system.

solution: Blood moves round the body inside blood vessels.

options: Q

P

explain.why: Q shows the windpipe, not the part asked about.

P shows the nose, not the part asked about.

solution: The two large organs filling the chest, on each side of the windpipe, are the lungs.

options: R

solution: The windpipe is the tube that leads down from the nose to the lungs.

options: R
S
P
Q

explain.why: R shows the lungs, not the part asked about.
S shows the windpipe, not the part asked about.
Q shows the nose, not the part asked about.

solution: The heart pumps blood. It sits between the lungs.

questions.stem: What is the job of the blood vessels?
options: To carry blood to and from different parts of the body
To let air pass in and out of the lungs when we breathe
To pump blood round the whole body
To break down food into digested food

explain.why: Air travels through the windpipe, not blood vessels.
The heart pumps the blood. Vessels only carry it.
This happens in the digestive system.

solution: Blood vessels are tubes that carry blood.

questions.stem: Which of the following does blood carry to the cells?
options: Carbon dioxide and waste from the gut
Oxygen and waste left after digestion
Carbon dioxide and digested food
Oxygen and digested food

explain.why: Neither is carried to the cells.
Undigested food stays in the gut and leaves as waste.
Carbon dioxide is carried away from the cells.

solution: Blood brings oxygen and digested food to the cells.

questions.stem: Which part of the body do humans use to take in oxygen from the air?
options: The lungs
The heart
The skin
The stomach

explain.why: The heart pumps blood.
Humans do not take in oxygen through the skin.
The stomach helps to digest food.

solution: Humans take in oxygen from the air with their lungs.

questions.stem: Which part of its body does a fish use to take in oxygen from the water?
options: Its gills
Its lungs
Its scales
Its fins

explain.why: Fish do not have lungs for breathing in water.
Scales cover and protect the body.
Fins help the fish to move.

solution: Fish take in oxygen that is dissolved in water through their gills.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a fish. Which letter shows the part that takes in oxygen from the water?
options: Q
R
P
S

explain.why: Q shows the tail, not the part asked about.
P shows the fin, not the part asked about.
S shows the eye, not the part asked about.

solution: The gills are just behind the head. Oxygen dissolved in the water passes into the blood there.

questions.stem: Which gas is more in the air a person breathes out than in the air the person breathes in?
options: Nitrogen
Oxygen
Carbon monoxide
Carbon dioxide

explain.why: Nitrogen is not used by the body, so it hardly changes.
There is less oxygen in the air breathed out.
Air we breathe out has almost no carbon monoxide.

solution: Cells make carbon dioxide, which is breathed out.

questions.stem: Which statement about plants and humans is correct?
options: Only plants give out carbon dioxide
Only humans need to take in oxygen
Both take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide
Plants take in carbon dioxide only and never take in oxygen

explain.why: Humans give out carbon dioxide too.
Plants also use oxygen for respiration.
Plants take in oxygen all day and night.

solution: Plants and humans both take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: The table compares the air a boy breathes in with the air he breathes out. Which gas is X?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Carbon monoxide
Nitrogen

explain.why: Oxygen is the gas that is less in the air breathed out.
Air has almost no carbon monoxide.
Nitrogen hardly changes.

solution: Gas X is more in the air breathed out, so it is carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How is water carried from the roots to the leaves of a plant?
options: By a heart in the roots
Through the air spaces around the roots
Through blood vessels in the stem
Through tubes in the stem

explain.why: Plants do not have a heart.
Water travels in tubes, not through air spaces.
Plants do not have blood.

solution: Plants have tubes that carry water.

questions.stem: What carries digested food to all parts of the human body?
options: Saliva
Blood
Air
Urine

explain.why: Saliva stays in the mouth.
Air carries oxygen into the lungs only.
Urine is waste, not a carrier of food.

solution: The blood carries digested food round the body.

questions.stem: Which statement about carrying substances in plants and humans is correct?
options: Only humans carry substances around the body
Both plants and humans use blood vessels
Plants use tubes and humans use blood vessels
Plants use blood vessels and humans use tubes

explain.why: Plants also carry water and food in tubes.
Plants do not have blood vessels.
Plants have tubes. Humans have blood vessels.

solution: Plants carry water and food in tubes, humans carry substances in blood vessels.

questions.stem: Which gas does blood carry away from the cells?
options: Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Oxygen
Carbon monoxide

explain.why: Cells do not make nitrogen.
Oxygen is carried to the cells.
Cells do not make carbon monoxide.

solution: Blood carries carbon dioxide from the cells to the lungs.

questions.stem: The diagram shows blood moving round the body. Which letter shows blood going from the heart to the body?
options: A
D
C
B

explain.why: A shows blood going from the heart to the lungs.
D shows blood coming back from the body to the heart.
B shows blood going from the lungs to the heart.

solution: Arrow C leaves the heart and goes to the body.

questions.stem: Which two systems work together to bring oxygen to the cells of the body?
options: The digestive system and the circulatory system together
The digestive system only
The respiratory system and the circulatory system
The digestive system and the respiratory system

explain.why: These two move food, not oxygen.
The digestive system takes in no oxygen.
The digestive system deals with food, not oxygen.

solution: The lungs take in oxygen and the blood carries it to the cells.

questions.stem: Which system breaks food down into digested food that the blood can carry?
options: The digestive system
The circulatory system
The skeleton
The respiratory system

explain.why: This system carries digested food but does not make it.
The skeleton supports the body.
This system takes in oxygen.

solution: Food is broken down by the digestive system.

questions.stem: Why do the cells of the body need digested food and oxygen?
options: To make the blood vessels longer
To release energy for the body to work
To help the blood vessels pump blood
To get rid of the carbon dioxide they make quickly

explain.why: Cells do not use them for that.
Blood vessels do not pump blood. The heart does.
Carbon dioxide is a waste gas made by cells.

solution: Cells use digested food and oxygen to release energy.

questions.stem: Which substance is made in the cells when they use digested food and oxygen to release energy?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Undigested food
Digested food

explain.why: Oxygen is used up, not made.
Undigested food never reaches the cells.
Digested food is used up.

solution: Cells give out carbon dioxide when they release energy.

questions.stem: After a meal, digested food reaches the rest of the body. Where does it go first after leaving the digestive system?
options: Out through the nose
Into the lungs
Into the windpipe
Into the blood

explain.why: Only air leaves by the nose.
The lungs deal with air.
The windpipe carries air.

solution: Digested food enters the blood, which carries it to the cells.

questions.stem: Which letter shows the part where oxygen from the air passes into the blood?
options: R
Q
S
P

explain.why: R shows the nose, not the part asked about.
Q shows the heart, not the part asked about.
P shows the windpipe, not the part asked about.

solution: Oxygen passes into the blood in the lungs.

questions.stem: Which of the following shows the path taken by air when a person breathes in through the nose?
options: Lungs, windpipe, nose
Windpipe, nose, lungs
Nose, lungs, windpipe
Nose, windpipe, lungs

explain.why: This is the path of air being breathed out.
Air enters through the nose first.
Air passes along the windpipe before it reaches the lungs.

solution: Air goes from the nose, down the windpipe, to the lungs.

questions.stem: Which pair of part and job is correct?
options: Blood vessels: pump blood back to the heart
Windpipe: passes oxygen into the blood
Heart: pumps blood to all parts of the body
Lungs: pump blood to all parts of the body

explain.why: Blood vessels carry blood but do not pump it.
The windpipe only carries air to the lungs.
Lungs take in oxygen. They do not pump blood.

solution: The heart is the pump of the circulatory system.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not carried by the blood?
options: Carbon dioxide
Digested food from the gut
Oxygen
Air from the nose

explain.why: Blood carries carbon dioxide away from the cells.
Blood carries digested food to the cells.
Blood carries oxygen to the cells.

solution: Air travels in the windpipe. The blood carries only oxygen, digested food and carbon dioxide from the list.

questions.stem: Which letter shows the part that carries air directly to the lungs?
options: Q
R
S
P

explain.why: R shows the heart, not the part asked about.
S shows the nose, not the part asked about.
P shows the lungs, not the part asked about.

solution: The windpipe leads straight into the lungs.

questions.stem: Mei puts her hand on her chest and breathes in deeply. What does she feel?
options: Her chest falls as her lungs fill with air
Her chest stays the same as air goes to her heart
Her chest rises as her lungs fill with air
Her chest falls as her lungs fill with blood

explain.why: The chest goes down when air is breathed out.
Air goes to the lungs, not the heart.
Lungs fill with air, not blood.

solution: The chest rises when we breathe in and falls when we breathe out.

questions.stem: Which statement about the heart is correct?
options: It breaks down food into digested food for the blood
It pumps blood through blood vessels to all parts of the body
It carries air along the windpipe to the nose
It takes in oxygen from the air and gives out carbon dioxide

explain.why: That is done in the digestive system.
The heart has nothing to do with the air passage.
That is the job of the lungs.

solution: The heart pumps blood round the body.

options: S
R
P
Q

explain.why: R shows the eye, not the part asked about.
P shows the tail, not the part asked about.
Q shows the fin, not the part asked about.

solution: Oxygen enters a fish's blood at its gills.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes how a fish gets oxygen?
options: Oxygen enters its blood through its scales
Air goes in its nose and down to its lungs
Water passes over its gills, where oxygen enters the blood
It swallows air bubbles that fill up its stomach and gut

explain.why: Scales do not take in oxygen.
Fish have gills, not lungs.
Air in the stomach does not reach the blood.

solution: A fish takes in dissolved oxygen through its gills.

questions.stem: The table shows how three living things take in oxygen. Which of the following correctly names X and Y?
options: X: fins, Y: windpipe
X: lungs, Y: gills
X: gills, Y: heart
X: gills, Y: lungs

explain.why: Neither part takes oxygen into the blood.
Fish use gills and humans use lungs.
The heart pumps blood.

solution: Fish use gills and humans use lungs.

options: They all use lungs to take in oxygen
They all take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide
They all give out carbon dioxide only at night
They all take in oxygen only from the air around them

explain.why: Fish have gills and plants have neither.
Living things give out carbon dioxide all the time.
Fish take in oxygen dissolved in water.

solution: All living things take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide for respiration.

questions.stem: The table shows three gases in the air a girl breathes in and out. Which gas is most likely to be Y?
options: Nitrogen
Oxygen
Carbon monoxide
Carbon dioxide

explain.why: Nitrogen stays about the same.
Oxygen goes down, not up, after breathing.
Air has almost no carbon monoxide.

solution: Y rises from 0.04% to 4%, so it is carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: A potted plant is kept in a dark room for a whole day. Does it take in oxygen?
options: Yes, because plants respire all the time
No, it takes in oxygen only when there is light
No, in the dark it takes in carbon dioxide instead
Yes, but only through its roots

explain.why: Plants respire all the time.
Taking in carbon dioxide does not replace oxygen use.
Leaves take in oxygen too.

solution: Plants respire all day, so they always take in oxygen.

questions.stem: A fish is taken out of the water and put on a dry table. It soon dies. Which is the best reason?
options: Its lungs fill up with air and cannot work
It cannot give out carbon dioxide through its nose
Its gills cannot take in enough oxygen from the air
Its blood vessels stop carrying food

explain.why: Fish do not have lungs.
Fish do not breathe through a nose.
Lack of oxygen is the cause.

solution: Gills are made to take oxygen from water, not from air.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the same for the transport systems of plants and humans?
options: Both carry oxygen and carbon dioxide in their tubes all the time
Both have a heart that pumps the liquid
Both have tubes that carry substances around the body
Both carry blood to every part

explain.why: Plant tubes carry water and food.
Plants do not have a heart.
Plants do not have blood.

solution: Plants have tubes and humans have blood vessels.

questions.stem: Which two substances are carried in the tubes of a plant?
options: Water and oxygen
Oxygen and carbon dioxide
Blood and water
Water and food

explain.why: Oxygen is not carried in them.
These are not carried in the plant's tubes.
Plants have no blood.

solution: The tubes of a plant carry water and food.

questions.stem: The table shows what blood carries. Which of the following correctly names P, Q and R?
options: P: carbon dioxide, Q: oxygen, R: digested food
P: digested food, Q: carbon dioxide, R: oxygen
P: oxygen, Q: digested food, R: carbon dioxide
P: oxygen, Q: carbon dioxide, R: digested food

explain.why: Oxygen goes from the lungs to the cells.
Digested food comes from the small intestine.
Carbon dioxide goes from the cells to the lungs.

solution: Blood carries oxygen from the lungs, carbon dioxide to the lungs and digested food from the small intestine.

questions.stem: Which statement about moving substances in plants and humans is correct?
options: In humans, substances move without blood vessels
In plants, a heart in the stem pushes water up
In both, the tubes carry only oxygen and carbon dioxide around the body
In humans, the heart pumps blood; plants do not have a heart

explain.why: Humans need blood vessels.
Plants do not have a heart.
Plant tubes carry water and food.

solution: Humans have a heart. Plants do not.

questions.stem: Which statement about blood is correct?
options: It carries digested food to the cells and carbon dioxide away from them
It carries undigested food to the cells and oxygen away from them
It carries air from the lungs to the cells and takes food away from the cells again
It carries oxygen away from the cells and carbon dioxide to them

explain.why: Cells get digested food, not undigested food.
Blood carries oxygen, not air.
Oxygen goes to the cells. Carbon dioxide goes away.

solution: Blood brings digested food and oxygen to the cells and takes carbon dioxide away.

questions.stem: After a meal, digested food passes into the blood vessels. Which system moves it to the muscles?
options: The digestive system
The respiratory system
The muscular system
The circulatory system

explain.why: It makes digested food but does not move it around the body.
This system carries air.
Muscles do not carry food round the body.

solution: The circulatory system carries digested food round the body.

questions.stem: A person cannot breathe for several minutes and becomes very ill. Which is the best reason?
options: The cells cannot make oxygen for themselves when needed
The heart cannot pump blood without any carbon dioxide
Oxygen cannot reach the cells, so they cannot release energy
Digested food cannot enter the blood vessels in the small intestine

explain.why: Cells never make oxygen.
Carbon dioxide is not needed for pumping.
Food enters blood in the small intestine.

solution: Without breathing, no oxygen reaches the cells.

questions.stem: In the diagram, which letter shows blood that has just taken in oxygen?
options: A
C
D
B

explain.why: A shows blood going from the heart to the lungs, so it has not yet taken in oxygen.
C shows blood going from the heart to the body, so it already carries oxygen but did not just take it in.
D shows blood coming back from the body.

solution: Blood takes in oxygen in the lungs, so arrow B from the lungs to the heart shows it.

options: His heart beat faster to bring in more air from outside
His heart beat faster to bring more oxygen to his muscles
His blood vessels became shorter
His lungs pumped his blood faster

explain.why: Air comes in through the nose.
Vessels do not change length.
The heart pumps the blood.

solution: The heart beat faster so the blood could bring more oxygen and digested food to the muscles.

questions.stem: Where do oxygen and digested food enter the blood?
options: Oxygen at the small intestine and digested food at the lungs
Both at the lungs
Both at the heart
Oxygen at the lungs and digested food at the small intestine

explain.why: These are the wrong way round.
Food enters blood in the small intestine.
The heart only pumps blood.

solution: Oxygen enters at the lungs. Digested food enters at the small intestine.

questions.stem: What happens to the carbon dioxide made by the cells of a leg muscle?
options: Blood carries it to the heart, where it is stored
Blood carries it to the stomach, where it is broken down and digested
It stays in the muscle cells until they are used up
Blood carries it to the lungs, where it is breathed out

explain.why: The heart does not store gases.
Gases are not digested.
The body must get rid of it.

solution: Carbon dioxide goes in the blood to the lungs and out through the nose.

questions.stem: Which statement about parts P, Q, R and S is correct?
options: P carries air to S, where digested food enters the blood
Q carries air from P to R, where oxygen enters the blood
S pumps air along Q to R, where carbon dioxide is made
R carries air from Q to P, where oxygen leaves the blood

explain.why: The heart takes in no food.
The heart pumps blood, not air.
Air goes from the nose down to the lungs.

solution: P is the nose, Q the windpipe, R the lungs and S the heart.

questions.stem: A piece of food blocks Sam's windpipe. Which is the most direct result?
options: Blood cannot reach the lungs, so the heart stops
Carbon dioxide cannot leave the cells, so oxygen is made
Digested food cannot reach the cells, so energy is lost
Air cannot reach the lungs, so oxygen cannot enter the blood

explain.why: The blood vessels are not blocked.
Cells never make oxygen.
Food is not carried in the windpipe.

solution: The windpipe is the air passage to the lungs.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly compares the heart and the lungs?
options: The heart takes in air; the lungs pump blood to the cells
The heart pumps blood round the body; the lungs take oxygen into the blood
The heart gives out carbon dioxide; the lungs make blood
The heart carries oxygen; the lungs carry digested food

explain.why: The jobs are the wrong way round.
The heart gives out no gas.
Both statements are wrong.

solution: The heart pumps. The lungs pass oxygen into the blood.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a person's heart stopped pumping?
options: Blood vessels would carry air instead, so the cells would keep working
Blood would stop moving, so cells would get no oxygen or digested food
Air would stop entering the nose, so the lungs would fill with blood
Digested food would stop forming, so the cells would make oxygen

explain.why: Blood vessels never carry air.
Air would still enter, but it would not be carried.
Cells never make oxygen.

solution: The heart pumps blood. If it stops, oxygen and digested food cannot reach the cells.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a fish. Which letter shows the part used to take in oxygen, and what else passes through it?
options: P; carbon dioxide also leaves the blood through it
R; carbon dioxide also leaves the blood through it
Q; only oxygen can pass through it
Q; carbon dioxide also leaves the blood through it

explain.why: P is the eye.
R is the tail.
Carbon dioxide leaves through the gills as well.

options: It takes in oxygen only through its roots and uses its leaves for carbon dioxide

It takes in oxygen from the air around its leaves and roots
It takes in oxygen only at night through its leaves

Plants respire all day and night.

solution: Plants take in oxygen from the air, through leaves and roots.

A human has lungs, so it is P.

solution: Humans have lungs, fish have gills and plants have neither.

options: The tubes in the roots, stem and leaves
The air spaces in the leaves, which carry blood
The flowers, which carry food to the roots
The roots, which pump water up to the leaves

explain.why: Plants do not have blood.

Roots do not pump.

solution: The tubes of a plant carry water and food, like blood vessels.

questions.stem: Why must blood vessels reach every part of the human body?
options: So that digested food is broken down in every vessel
So that the heart can take in air from every part
So that every cell gets oxygen and digested food and loses carbon dioxide
So that blood can leave the body with the carbon dioxide

explain.why: Food is digested in the digestive system.
The heart takes in no air.
Blood stays inside; carbon dioxide leaves in the breath.

solution: Every cell needs a supply of oxygen and digested food and a way to lose carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: The bar graph shows the oxygen in blood at three places. Which statement explains the difference between the first two bars?
options: Digested food in the lungs adds oxygen to the blood
Oxygen passes out of the blood as it flows through the lungs
The heart makes oxygen and adds it to the blood
Oxygen passes into the blood as it flows through the lungs

explain.why: Oxygen comes from the air.
Blood gains oxygen in the lungs.
The heart only pumps blood.

solution: The blood leaving the lungs has more oxygen because it took it in from the air.

questions.stem: Why do people need to eat and to breathe in order to run?
options: The blood brings digested food and oxygen to muscle cells, which use them to release energy
The blood takes carbon dioxide to the muscles, which release it as energy
The lungs bring digested food and oxygen to muscle cells, which make energy
The blood brings food and air to the muscle cells, which store them as energy

explain.why: Carbon dioxide is waste.
Blood carries them; the lungs do not.
Cells use oxygen and digested food, not air, to release energy.

solution: Digested food and oxygen reach the cells in the blood and are used to release energy.

questions.stem: A patient's small intestine cannot pass digested food into the blood. What is the most direct effect?
options: The cells receive less oxygen from the lungs
The lungs cannot take in air through the windpipe
Less of the food the body can use reaches the cells
The blood cannot carry carbon dioxide to the lungs

explain.why: The lungs are not affected.
The air passage is not affected.
Carbon dioxide is still carried.

solution: Digested food reaches the cells only after it enters the blood.

questions.stem: The blood vessels in a man's leg are partly blocked, so less blood reaches the leg. What is most likely to happen to the cells of his leg?
options: They get the same oxygen, but less digested food
They get less oxygen and digested food, and carbon dioxide builds up
They get more oxygen, but less carbon dioxide builds up
They get less carbon dioxide, so they release more energy

explain.why: Both are carried by the blood.
Less blood brings less oxygen.
With less supply they release less energy.

solution: Less blood means less oxygen and food in and less carbon dioxide taken away.

questions.stem: Which statement links the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems?
options: Digested food and oxygen are both taken in by the lungs and carried by the heart alone
Digested food and oxygen are taken in by two systems and carried to the cells by the third
Carbon dioxide is taken in by the lungs and carried to the cells as food
Oxygen is made by the digestive system and carried by the lungs to the cells

explain.why: Food does not enter at the lungs.
Carbon dioxide is a waste gas.
No system makes oxygen.

solution: The digestive and respiratory systems take in food and oxygen; the circulatory system carries them to the cells.

questions.stem: The diagram shows how blood moves between the lungs, the heart and the body. Which two arrows carry blood that contains the most oxygen?
options: A and B
C and D
B and C
A and D

explain.why: A carries blood from the heart to the lungs, which has little oxygen.
D carries blood from the body to the heart, which has little oxygen.
Both carry blood that has little oxygen.

solution: Blood takes in oxygen in the lungs and goes along B to the heart. The heart pumps it along C to the body.
